# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## An international expansion framework for a European sustainable apparel business
**Board / Executive Committee decision document | v1.0**
**Decision sought: adoption of the *two-track structure*, the beachhead selection method, the gate sequence, and funding of Gate 0. All quantities are calibrated at Gate 0/1 and returned to this Committee for approval.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop treating "expand into a new region" as one decision.** Demand entry and supply entry are two different problems with different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different people running them — and forcing them into the same geography is how mid-sized brands destroy margin in both. Adopt a **two-track model**: a **Demand Track** entering **Japan as a beachhead** (highest willingness-to-pay for material provenance, the lowest apparel return rate of any major market, a wholesale channel that lets us buy market intelligence with someone else's working capital, and a domestic repair-and-resale culture that makes our circularity story native rather than imported), with **South Korea as a fast-follow at Month [30]**; and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam as primary new-origin manufacturing**, with **India retained for certified organic cotton fibre and fabric** and **Portugal/Turkey retained as nearshore replenishment**. The two tracks are decoupled operationally but joined at exactly one place — the **Origin Bridge (§3.2)**: Vietnam is, we believe, the only new sourcing origin that is duty-advantaged into *both* the EU (EVFTA) and Japan (CPTPP/RCEP/AJCEP), which converts a sourcing decision into a market-access asset instead of a tariff liability. Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics" — Japan already has Uniqlo and Muji and will beat us at that forever (§5). Channels are sequenced credibility-first, capital-last (§6). **One constraint governs everything: the Substantiation Rule (§2.1) — no claim travels faster than its evidence, and no volume travels faster than its audit.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every share, cost, margin, headcount and threshold in this document is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use in each section. They are here because a strategy with no numbers cannot be argued with, and an unarguable strategy cannot be improved. **Gate 0 (§15) replaces them with researched values; Gate 1 replaces those with contracted values.**

Three categories of figure carry different confidence:

| Type | Example | Confidence | Resolved at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, labelling statute, entity threshold | Should be certain — verify, do not estimate | Gate 0, by counsel |
| **Researchable quantity** | Market size, AOV, competitor pricing, CAC benchmark | Estimable to ±[20]% | Gate 0, by field research |
| **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, our channel mix, our vendor count | A choice, not a discovery | Gate 1, by this Committee |

**Anything in this document touching tariff preference, rules of origin, GSP eligibility or labelling law is a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact.** Trade preference regimes graduate, expire and change; a strategy built on a lapsed preference is a strategy built on nothing.

### 0.2 What we are asking the Committee to adopt today

The two-track structure (§3); the market-selection criteria and weights (§4); the positioning boundary (§5.2); the channel sequence and its capital discipline (§6); the vendor qualification standard (§9.2); the decision-rights matrix (Appendix B); the gate sequence with its **kill criteria** (§14.4, §15); and €[350–500]k to fund Gate 0.

We are **not** asking for approval of the full investment envelope, the beachhead country as an irrevocable choice, or any hiring beyond the Gate 0 team.

### 0.3 Who and what this covers

| In scope | Out of scope (this document) |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered via one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiation of existing Portuguese/Turkish vendor terms |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | M&A, licensing-out, franchising |
| Sustainability substantiation infrastructure (which we need anyway) | Product architecture redesign beyond market-fit adaptation |

**Rule of the document:** every commitment made to the new market has a stated cost to the core business — management attention, working capital, or inventory risk. Expansion strategies fail in the home market more often than in the target market, and they fail silently.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The question has been framed as *"which country next?"* That is the wrong axis, because country is a **consequence** of what we are trying to buy.

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**, and where is it neither? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, defect rate, lead-time inventory and audit overhead** — and is it actually lower? |
| Should we go DTC or wholesale? | What is the cheapest way to buy market truth before we commit capital that cannot be recovered? |
| How do we translate our brand? | Which of our claims survive contact with a market that has better craft literacy than our home market? |

**Corollary 1 — Cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in the landed-cost equation. A [15]% FOB saving is erased by an [11]% duty, a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, a [2]-point defect rate, or one supply-chain labour finding that costs us a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are **landed-cost-after-risk** decisions or they are guesses.

**Corollary 2 — Most "international expansion failure" is domestic.** It is under-resourced management attention, working cap
